tool.name: Docker
tool.tagline: Build, ship and run applications in portable containers
tool.description: Docker packages an application and everything it needs into an image that runs the same way on a laptop, a CI runner or a production server. It is the standard way to build and run containers, and the foundation for Compose-based development environments and Kubernetes deployments.

glossary.def: Docker's app for Mac and Windows. It installs everything Docker needs, including a small hidden Linux virtual machine where your containers actually run.
The core of Docker on Linux: the background program that builds images and runs containers, plus the docker command you type to control it.
The background program that does Docker's real work: downloading images, building them and starting and stopping containers. The docker command only passes your requests to it.
Docker's public online library of images, and the place Docker downloads from when an image name doesn't say otherwise (docker.io).
The thin, initially empty layer Docker puts on top of an image for each container. Every file the container creates or changes goes here, and it is deleted with the container.
An image's fingerprint, like sha256:4f1c..., calculated from its exact contents. Unlike a tag it can never point to anything else, so it names one exact image.
In Docker, the label after the colon in an image name, such as 1.27 in nginx:1.27, usually naming a version. It can later be moved to a different image.
An image left with no name, shown as <none>:<none>, usually because a newer build took over its tag. Safe to remove unless a container uses it.
Writing a Dockerfile command as plain text, like CMD python app.py. Docker runs it through a shell, which then becomes the main process instead of your program.
A Dockerfile with several FROM sections (stages): early stages build the program with all the tools that needs, and only the finished result is copied into the small final image.

In Docker: docker exec runs an extra command inside a container that is already running. The exec form writes a Dockerfile command as a bracketed list, like CMD ["python", "app.py"], so it starts directly, without a shell in between.
Docker's modern build engine, used by docker build. It skips steps it doesn't need, runs independent ones at the same time, and adds extras such as cache and secret mounts.
A storage area managed by Docker that lives outside any container and is attached to a folder inside one, so data such as a database's files survives when the container is deleted.
A Docker volume created without a name (it gets a random ID). Easy to lose track of; removed with its container only when you use --rm or docker rm -v.
Making a real folder or file of the host appear inside a container at a chosen path. Both sides see the same files, so changes show up instantly on both.
A folder in a container that is kept only in memory: very fast, never written to disk, and emptied when the container stops.
A private network Docker creates on one host so containers can talk to each other. On networks you create yourself, containers can find each other by name.
A Linux namespace that maps user IDs inside a container to different ones on the host, so the container's administrator is an ordinary, powerless user outside it.
A Linux file system feature that stacks several folders so they look like one. Docker uses it to place a container's writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers.
What overlayfs does the first time a container changes a file that came from the image: it copies the whole file into the container's writable layer, then changes the copy.
A special marker in an upper layer saying 'this file is deleted'. It hides the file from view, but the data still sits in the lower layer.
A small file in a registry that lists one image per platform (for example linux/amd64 and linux/arm64) under a single name, so each computer downloads the one it can run.
The file that describes one image: it points, by fingerprint, to the image's settings file and to each of its layers.
One image name that holds versions for several kinds of processor (such as Intel/AMD and ARM), so Macs, PCs and servers each get the version they can run.
The background program, underneath the Docker daemon, that manages images and keeps containers running. Kubernetes can use it directly, without Docker.
The small low-level program that actually creates a container, setting up its namespaces and limits, starts its main process and then exits.
The administrator's powers on Linux split into separate permissions (change file owners, use low ports, change network settings...), so a process can be given only the ones it needs.
Running the Docker daemon itself as an ordinary user rather than as the administrator, so even a container that breaks out of its walls gets only that user's rights.
A program that imitates a different kind of processor in software, so a computer can run programs built for another one (for example ARM programs on an Intel PC), only much more slowly.
A software bill of materials: a list of every package and version inside a piece of software, used to check it for known security problems.
One slice of an image: the files added, changed or deleted by one build step. An image is a stack of these, they never change, and images that start the same way share their bottom layers.
The results of earlier image-building steps that Docker keeps so it can reuse them instead of redoing the work. Deleting it is safe; the next build is just slower.
A Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own private view of one thing, such as the list of running processes or the network. Containers are built from several of them.
A very small image that contains only what an app needs to run: no shell, no package installer and no other operating system tools.
Docker's built-in tool for running containers across several computers as one group. Less common today than Kubernetes.
A BuildKit feature that lends a secret file (a password, a key) to one RUN step during a build without saving it anywhere in the image.
A BuildKit feature that keeps a folder, such as a package installer's download folder, between builds without putting it in the image, so reinstalls are fast.
A tiny helper program, one per container, that stays as the container's parent after runc exits, so Docker's own background programs can restart without stopping containers.
A small program that stores registry passwords and tokens in your operating system's secure password store instead of a plain text file.
The private connection point (/var/run/docker.sock) through which the docker command talks to the Docker daemon. Anyone who can use it controls Docker, and so the host.
A plain text file of step-by-step instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD...) that Docker follows to build an image.
The existing image a Dockerfile starts from with its FROM line, such as python:3.13-slim. Your own steps are added on top of it.
The folder you hand to docker build (often just .). The build can copy files only from inside it.
Docker's tool for describing several containers (an app, its database, a cache...) in one compose.yaml file and starting or stopping them all with docker compose up and down.
A container setting (--restart) that tells Docker whether to start it again automatically after it stops or the computer restarts: no, on-failure, always or unless-stopped.

concepts.name: Containers vs virtual machines
concepts.summary: A virtual machine imitates a whole computer; a container is one walled-off program sharing your real one. That's why containers start instantly.
concepts.why: Knowing what a container really is tells you what to expect from it: how fast it starts, how well it's walled off, and where it can run.
concepts.body:
Every computer runs an **operating system**: Windows, macOS or Linux. It's the software that starts first when you switch the machine on, and it shares the computer out among all the other programs. Its innermost part, the one that controls the hardware, is the **kernel**.

When you open an app, the operating system starts a **process**: one running copy of the program, with its own share of **memory** (the fast, short-term space where running programs keep their data). Normally every process sees the same files and all the other processes.

To wall an app off from everything else, there are two approaches.

A **virtual machine** (VM) is a whole pretend computer inside your real one, with its own operating system that starts up from scratch. The program that creates and runs VMs is called a **hypervisor**. VMs are strongly walled off, but heavy: each takes a big, fixed share of memory and tens of seconds to start.

A **container** is much lighter. It's an ordinary process walled into its own private corner of the computer, with its own files, its own network address and its own list of programs. From inside, it can't see anything else running, so it acts as if it had the computer to itself.

There's no second operating system inside. Every container shares the kernel of the real computer underneath, called the **host**; the walls come from features built into Linux. Nothing has to start up, so a container launches in a fraction of a second, and one host can run hundreds.

What that buys you:

- **Packaging**: the app travels with everything it needs, so it runs the same on your laptop and on a **server** (a computer that runs programs for others, like the ones behind a website).
- **Side by side**: apps that need different versions of the same tool share one computer without clashing.
- **Throwaway**: containers are cheap to create and delete, so you replace a broken one rather than repair it.

The shared kernel has a price. Linux containers need a Linux kernel, so on a Mac or Windows PC, **Docker Desktop** quietly runs a small Linux VM to hold them. And the walls are thinner than a VM's: a flaw in the shared kernel can affect every container on the host.

So the two aren't rivals: computers you rent over the internet (**the cloud**) are usually VMs, with your containers running inside them.
takeaways: A container is a walled-off process that shares the host's kernel
A VM is a pretend computer with its own complete operating system
Containers start in a fraction of a second and are light, but are walled off less strongly than VMs
On Mac and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your containers inside a hidden Linux VM
pitfalls: Treating a container like a little computer you log into and repair by hand: throw it away and start a fresh, updated one instead.

quiz.q: Why can a container start in a fraction of a second while a VM takes much longer?
options: A container is just a process on the host's already-running kernel, so no operating system has to start
Container files are smaller, so they download faster
VMs have to be downloaded again every time they start
quiz.explain: A VM starts a whole operating system; a container is only a walled-off process on a kernel that is already running.

quiz.q: How do Linux containers run on a Mac with Docker Desktop?
options: macOS can run Linux programs directly
Docker rewrites each Linux program for macOS
Inside a small Linux virtual machine that Docker Desktop manages
They can't; only Mac containers run on a Mac
quiz.explain: Containers need a Linux kernel to share, so Docker Desktop provides one inside a small VM.

concepts.name: Install Docker and run hello-world
concepts.summary: Install Docker, check it works with docker version, and run your first container.
concepts.why: Every later lesson types Docker commands, and knowing Docker's two halves explains the most common setup error.
concepts.body:
You use Docker by typing commands into a **terminal**: a window where you type a line of text, press Enter, and the computer runs it and prints the result. On a Mac it's the Terminal app; on Windows, PowerShell. A program you control this way is called a **command-line tool** (or CLI). Every command in these lessons starts with the word `docker`.

Docker comes in two halves. The `docker` command you type is only the **client**: it passes your instructions on. The real work, such as starting and stopping containers, is done by the **Docker daemon** (`dockerd`), a program that runs quietly in the background all the time, waiting for instructions. That makes the daemon a kind of server, and the two halves talk over a private connection on your computer.

How to install:

- **Mac and Windows**: install Docker Desktop from docker.com. It contains the client, the daemon, the small Linux VM your containers run in, and a window with buttons for the same tasks.
- **Linux**: install **Docker Engine** (the daemon plus the client) by following the steps for your Linux version at docs.docker.com. Use Docker's own instructions: the copy offered by Linux's built-in app store is often years out of date.

Check it with `docker version`. It prints two sections, **Client** and **Server** (the daemon). If the Server part says "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon", the client works but can't reach the daemon: it isn't running (start Docker Desktop) or you lack permission (see below).

Then run the classic first test, `docker run hello-world`. Docker looks on your computer for a ready-made package called `hello-world`, doesn't find it, downloads it from **Docker Hub** (Docker's public online collection of such packages), and starts a container from it. The container prints a greeting and stops. These packages are called images; the next lesson explains them.

On Linux, Docker commands at first need administrator rights, so you type **`sudo`** in front of them: it runs one command as the administrator, after asking for your password. Adding your user account to the `docker` group (a list of users Linux grants extra permissions) removes that need, but understand what it means: whoever can give orders to the daemon can take over the whole computer, because the daemon runs as administrator and can start a container that reaches every file. Rootless mode, covered much later, avoids this.
concepts.code:
docker version
# Client: Version: 29.x ...
# Server: Docker Engine - Community  Version: 29.x ...

docker run hello-world
# Unable to find image 'hello-world:latest' locally
# latest: Pulling from library/hello-world
# Hello from Docker!

# A one-line summary from the daemon (its version and how it stores files)
docker info --format '{{.ServerVersion}} {{.Driver}}'

# Linux only: use docker without sudo (gives full control of the computer!)
sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER" && newgrp docker
takeaways: You type docker commands in a terminal; the docker client passes them to the Docker daemon, which does the work
docker version shows both halves; an error in the Server part means the daemon isn't running or can't be reached
On Linux, membership of the docker group is as powerful as the administrator password
pitfalls: Installing the outdated Docker copy from Linux's built-in app store instead of following Docker's own instructions, then finding newer commands such as docker compose missing.

quiz.q: docker version prints the Client section, then 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon'. What's wrong?
options: The hello-world image hasn't been downloaded yet
The daemon isn't running, or you don't have permission to reach it
quiz.explain: The client works (it printed its section); it just can't reach dockerd.

quiz.q: Why is adding a user to the docker group a security decision?
options: It turns off the computer's network protection
Whoever controls the daemon can start containers that read and change every file on the computer
It shares your Docker Hub password
It removes the walls around containers
quiz.explain: The daemon runs as administrator, so whoever can give it orders effectively has administrator rights too.

concepts.name: Images and containers
concepts.summary: An image is a read-only package of an app and all its files; a container is one running copy made from it.
concepts.why: Every Docker command works on either images or containers, so telling them apart avoids most beginner confusion.
concepts.body:
An **image** is a packaged, ready-to-run copy of an app. It holds every file the app needs (the app itself, the tools it relies on, a stripped-down set of Linux basics) plus a few settings, such as which command to run when it starts. Think of it as a frozen copy of a tidy computer with the app already installed.

Images never change once built: they're **read-only**. They're made of **read-only layers** stacked like transparent sheets: say, one sheet with the Linux basics, one adding Python (a programming language), one adding your app. Images that start with the same bottom layers share them instead of storing them twice.

A **container** is a running copy of an image. Docker lays a thin, empty **writable layer** on top of the image's layers, so the container can create and change files, then starts the image's command as a walled-off process. You can start many containers from one image, like baking many cakes from one recipe: they share the image's layers, and each gets its own writable layer.

Delete a container and its writable layer goes too, with every file the container created. The image is untouched, so the next container starts clean. (Keeping data across containers comes later, with volumes.)

Images are stored in a **registry**, an online store you download them from; Docker Hub is the default. An image's full name says where it lives: `registry/account/name:tag`.

- `nginx:1.27` is short for `docker.io/library/nginx:1.27`: Docker Hub (`docker.io`), Docker's official collection (`library`), the nginx website program, version `1.27`.
- `ghcr.io/acme/api:2.3.1` lives on a different registry, `ghcr.io`.
- The part after the colon is the **tag**, a label usually naming a version. Leave it out and you get `:latest`, which is just the default label, not a promise of the newest version.

Tags aren't fixed: tomorrow someone could put the label `1.27` on a different image. So each image also has a fingerprint that can't change, its **image digest**, such as `nginx@sha256:4f1c...`. It's calculated from the image's exact contents, so the same digest always means exactly the same image.

`docker pull` downloads an image; `docker run` downloads it for you if needed. Images arrive layer by layer, and layers you already have are skipped.
concepts.code:
docker pull nginx:1.27                 # download an image
docker image ls nginx
# REPOSITORY  TAG   IMAGE ID      CREATED      SIZE
# nginx       1.27  9bea9f2796e2  2 weeks ago  192MB

docker run -d --name web1 nginx:1.27   # two containers (-d: in the background),
docker run -d --name web2 nginx:1.27   # one image
docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Image}}'
# web2 nginx:1.27
# web1 nginx:1.27

# The image's digest (its unchangeable fingerprint)
docker image inspect nginx:1.27 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
# nginx@sha256:...
takeaways: Image = read-only, layered package; container = a running copy plus its own writable layer
Many containers can share one image
Full name: registry/account/name:tag; :latest is only a default tag
Tags can be changed; a digest always names the exact same image
pitfalls: Assuming :latest means the newest release: it's whatever was last uploaded with that tag, or nothing at all.

quiz.q: You create files inside a container, then remove the container. What happens to the files?
options: They are saved into the image
They are lost along with the container's writable layer
They move to the next container started from the image
They are uploaded to the registry
quiz.explain: A container's changes live in its own writable layer, which is deleted with it (volumes, covered later, keep data).

quiz.q: What does docker run postgres refer to, if you give nothing else?
options: The newest postgres version ever published
A postgres container that is already running
postgres installed by your computer's app store
quiz.explain: Docker Hub, Docker's official collection (library) and the latest tag are the defaults.

concepts.name: Running containers with docker run
concepts.summary: Start containers in the foreground or background, name them, type into them, and swap the command they run.
concepts.why: docker run is the command you'll use most, and its options decide how the container behaves.
concepts.body:
`docker run [options] IMAGE [COMMAND]` makes a new container from an image and starts it. The extra words starting with a dash are options, which change how a command behaves. The most useful ones:

- `-d` (detached): run in the background and give you your terminal back. Without it, the container's output fills your terminal and Ctrl+C stops it.
- `--name api`: give the container a name you choose, instead of a random one like `quirky_turing`. Names must be unique.
- `-it`: let you type into the container, as if sitting at its keyboard. You use it to get a **shell** (the program that reads typed commands and runs them, the thing behind every terminal) inside the container: `docker run -it ubuntu bash` starts `bash`, a common shell, in a container made from the `ubuntu` image (Ubuntu is a popular Linux version).
- `--rm`: delete the container automatically when it stops. Great for one-off commands.
- `-e KEY=value`: set an **environment variable**, a named setting handed to the app when it starts, such as `-e NAME=Ada`.

Two more options, `-p` for network access and `-v` for storage, come in later lessons.

Anything you type after the image name **replaces the image's default command**. `docker run python:3.13 python -c "print(42)"` runs that small Python command, which prints 42, instead of whatever the python image normally starts.

The rule that surprises everyone: **a container lives exactly as long as its main process**. The command it starts with is process number 1 inside the container. That number is its **process ID**, written PID, so the main process is "PID 1". When that command finishes, the container stops. That's why `docker run -d ubuntu` stops at once: its default command is the `bash` shell, which ends immediately when nobody is typing into it. Think of a container as one running program, not a computer you leave switched on.

Every `docker run` makes a **new** container. To start an existing stopped one again, use `docker start`. Using `--rm` for experiments keeps old containers from piling up.
concepts.code:
docker run --rm alpine echo "hello"       # hello (container deleted afterwards)
docker run -it --rm ubuntu:24.04 bash     # a shell inside; type exit to leave
docker run -d --name cache redis:7        # a database, running in the background
docker run --rm -e NAME=Ada python:3.13 \
  python -c "import os; print('hi', os.environ['NAME'])"   # hi Ada

docker run -d ubuntu:24.04                # stops at once: no one is typing into bash
docker ps -a --format '{{.Image}} {{.Status}}'
# ubuntu:24.04  Exited (0) 2 seconds ago
# redis:7       Up 10 seconds
takeaways: -d for background, --name to name it, -it to type into it, --rm to clean up afterwards
Words after the image name replace its default command
A container stops when its main process (PID 1) ends
docker run always makes a new container; docker start restarts an old one
pitfalls: Putting options after the image name: docker run alpine --rm hands --rm to the container's command, not to Docker.

quiz.q: You run docker run -d ubuntu and it stops immediately. Why?
options: Ubuntu images need a license key
Its default command, the bash shell, ends at once when nobody is typing into it, so the container stops
quiz.explain: A container lives only as long as its main process.

quiz.q: What does docker run nginx:1.27 echo hi do?
options: Starts nginx and also prints hi
Prints hi instead of starting nginx
Fails, because nginx has no echo
quiz.explain: Words after the image name replace the image's default command.

concepts.name: Managing containers: ps, logs, exec, stop
concepts.summary: List containers, read what they print, open a shell inside them, and stop, restart or remove them.
concepts.why: Day-to-day work with containers is mostly these commands.
concepts.body:
Once containers are running you need to see and control them. Every container has an ID (a long random code; its first few characters are enough) and a name, and these commands accept either.

Seeing what's going on:

- `docker ps` lists running containers; `docker ps -a` includes stopped ones.
- `docker logs api` shows everything the app has printed. Programs have two separate outputs, **standard output** for normal messages and **standard error** for problems, and Docker keeps both. `-f` keeps following new lines; `--tail 100` shows only the last 100.
- `docker exec -it api sh` starts an **extra** process inside a running container, here the `sh` shell, so you can look around. Type `exit` to leave. It only works while the container is running.

Because `docker logs` shows only what was printed, apps in containers should print their **log messages** (the running notes an app writes about what it's doing) instead of saving them to files inside the container.

Stopping and cleaning up:

- `docker stop api` politely asks the main process to finish by sending it **SIGTERM**, a standard "please stop" message. If it's still running 10 seconds later, Docker sends **SIGKILL**, which ends it instantly. Well-written apps react to SIGTERM by finishing their current work and closing cleanly.
- `docker kill api` sends SIGKILL straight away.
- `docker start api` and `docker restart api` start a stopped container again, with its files intact.
- `docker rm api` deletes a stopped container; `docker rm -f api` stops and deletes it.
- Stopped containers stay until removed, so `docker ps -a` keeps growing. `docker container prune` removes all stopped ones at once.

Details:

- `docker inspect api` prints everything Docker knows about a container, including its state and its **exit code**: the number a program reports when it ends, where 0 means success and anything else means something went wrong. The output is **JSON**, a common text format of labelled values; `--format` picks out one value.
- `docker stats` shows, live, how much memory and processor power (**CPU**) each container is using.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api python:3.13 python -m http.server   # a tiny website program
docker ps                         # running containers
docker logs -f --tail 20 api      # follow its output (Ctrl+C stops following)
docker exec -it api bash          # a shell inside; type exit to leave
docker exec api ls /              # run one command inside
docker inspect api --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}'
docker stop api                   # SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds
docker ps -a --filter name=api    # Exited (...)
docker start api && docker restart api
docker rm -f api
docker container prune            # remove all stopped containers
takeaways: ps lists; logs shows what the app printed; exec runs an extra process inside
stop sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 seconds
Stopped containers stay until docker rm or prune
inspect --format pulls any detail out of the JSON
pitfalls: Expecting docker logs to show files the app writes inside the container: it only shows what the app prints (standard output and standard error).

quiz.q: What does docker stop do first?
options: Sends SIGTERM and waits a few seconds for the app to finish
quiz.explain: SIGTERM lets the app close cleanly; SIGKILL follows only if it doesn't stop in time.

quiz.q: Which command opens a shell inside an already running container named db?
quiz.explain: exec runs a new process in an existing container; run would create a new container.

concepts.name: Managing images and disk space
concepts.summary: List, tag and remove images, and win back space on your disk with docker system df and prune.
concepts.why: Images and Docker's leftovers quietly fill tens of gigabytes; knowing how to clean up keeps your computer healthy.
concepts.body:
Every image you pull or build stays on your computer's **disk** (its long-term storage, where files stay when the power is off) until you remove it. So do stopped containers and Docker's other leftovers. Images are large, so after a few months Docker can easily take up tens of **gigabytes** (GB), as much as thousands of photos.

Looking at images:

- `docker image ls` (or `docker images`): name, tag, ID and size of each image.
- `docker image history nginx:1.27`: the image's layers and the size of each.
- `docker tag nginx:1.27 myreg.example.com/nginx:prod`: give an image a second name. A tag is just a label; nothing is copied.

When you build a new version of an image under the same tag (you'll build your own soon), the tag goes to the new image and the old one is left without a name, listed as `<none>:<none>`. These leftovers are called **dangling images**; `docker image ls --filter dangling=true` lists them.

Removing:

- `docker rmi nginx:1.27` (or `docker image rm`) removes that name, and the image itself once no other name or container uses it. An image used by a container, even a stopped one, needs `-f`.
- `docker image prune` removes dangling images; add `-a` to remove every image no container uses.

The big picture: `docker system df` shows how much space images, containers, volumes and the **Docker build cache** take, and how much you could win back. Volumes hold saved data, such as a database's files (a later lesson). That cache holds the results of earlier image-building steps, kept so Docker can reuse them; it's often the biggest item, and `docker builder prune` safely clears it.

`docker system prune` removes stopped containers, dangling images, the build cache and a few other unused things. Add `-a` to also remove every unused image, and `--volumes` to include unused volumes. Be careful with that last one: it can wipe out data such as your local database.
concepts.code:
docker image ls
docker image history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' python:3.13-slim | head -5
docker tag myapp:dev myapp:1.0.0       # second name, same image ID

docker system df
# TYPE           TOTAL  ACTIVE  SIZE     RECLAIMABLE
# Images         41     6       18.2GB   15.9GB (87%)
# Build Cache    312    0       9.4GB    9.4GB

docker image prune                     # dangling images only
docker builder prune --filter until=168h   # build cache older than a week
docker system prune -a                 # everything unused (not volumes)
takeaways: Tags are labels; one image can have many
Dangling images are nameless leftovers from rebuilds
docker system df shows where space goes; prune wins it back
Only prune volumes deliberately: they hold data
pitfalls: Running docker system prune -a --volumes on your own computer and wiping out your local databases.

quiz.q: You rebuilt myapp:dev several times and now see several <none> images. What are they?
options: Dangling images, left nameless when the tag moved to each newer build
quiz.explain: The tag moved to the new image each time, leaving the old ones without a name.

concepts.name: Dockerfile basics
concepts.summary: Write a Dockerfile with FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE and CMD to package your own app as an image.
concepts.why: A Dockerfile is the recipe for your image; every project that uses Docker has one.
concepts.body:
So far you've run images other people made. To package your own app you write a **Dockerfile**: a plain text file of instructions, one per line, that Docker follows from top to bottom to build an image. Each line starts with an instruction word in capitals.

The everyday instructions:

- `FROM python:3.13-slim`: the **base image** to start from, here a small image with Python already installed. Always first.
- `WORKDIR /app`: create the folder (or **directory**, the usual technical word) `/app` inside the image and make it the **working directory**, the folder that later instructions, and the running container, start in.
- `COPY requirements.txt .`: copy a file from your project folder into the image (`.` means "the current folder", here `/app`). Its cousin `ADD` can also download files and extract archive files; prefer `COPY` unless you need that.
- `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`: run a command **while building**, and keep its result in the image. Here it installs the **packages** the app needs (ready-made add-ons written by others), listed in `requirements.txt`.
- `ENV PORT=8000`: set an environment variable, both for the build and for every container.
- `EXPOSE 8000`: a note saying the app listens on **port** 8000. A port is a numbered door on a computer that network connections arrive through. `EXPOSE` is only a note; it opens nothing.
- `USER app`: run later steps, and the container, as the ordinary user `app` rather than as the all-powerful administrator.
- `CMD ["python", "app.py"]`: the default command when a container starts, here running the app's main Python file, `app.py`. If there are several, the last one wins.

`RUN` happens once, while the image is built; `CMD` happens every time a container starts. Mixing them up is the classic beginner bug.

Write `CMD` as a bracketed list, `CMD ["python", "app.py"]` (the **exec form**), not as plain text, `CMD python app.py` (the **shell form**). The shell form starts a shell that then starts your app, so the shell becomes PID 1. When `docker stop` sends SIGTERM, the shell receives it and doesn't pass it on: your app never hears "please stop" and is killed 10 seconds later.

`ENTRYPOINT` sets a fixed program to run, and `CMD` then supplies only its default **command-line arguments** (the extra words that follow a command). With `ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn"]` (a program that serves Python websites) and `CMD ["app:app"]`, `docker run img other:app` swaps just that last part. Use it when an image exists to run one program.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile
# Start from a small image that already has Python
FROM python:3.13-slim
# Work inside /app from here on
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
# Build time: install the add-ons listed in requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
# Then copy the rest of the project
COPY . .
ENV PORT=8000
# Only a note: the app listens on port 8000
EXPOSE 8000
# Create an ordinary user called app and switch to it
RUN useradd --create-home app
USER app
# Run time: the command each container starts with
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
takeaways: RUN runs while building; CMD is the default command each time a container starts
Write CMD in exec form, `["cmd", "arg"]`, so your app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
EXPOSE is only a note; the port is opened at docker run
`ENTRYPOINT` fixes the program; `CMD` supplies the words that follow it
pitfalls: Writing RUN python app.py to 'start' the app: it runs during the build, which then hangs or finishes with nothing useful saved.

quiz.q: When does a RUN instruction execute?
options: Once, while the image is being built
Only when you run docker exec
When the image is uploaded to a registry
quiz.explain: RUN's result is saved in the image; CMD is what runs each time a container starts.

quiz.q: Why prefer CMD ["node", "server.js"] over CMD node server.js?
options: The plain-text form is no longer allowed
The bracketed form makes the image smaller
The bracketed (exec) form makes node PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM from docker stop
The plain-text form can't read environment variables
quiz.explain: The shell form wraps the command in a shell (/bin/sh -c), which usually doesn't pass SIGTERM on.

concepts.name: Building and tagging images
concepts.summary: Turn a Dockerfile into an image with docker build, understand the build context, and name versions well.
concepts.why: Building and naming images well is the bridge between your code and the computers that will run it.
concepts.body:
`docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` builds an image from the file named `Dockerfile` in the folder you're in, and names it `myapp:1.0` (`-t` stands for tag).

The final `.` is the **build context**: the folder whose files the build may use. `COPY` paths start from it, and nothing outside it can be copied: `COPY ../secret .` fails, since `..` means "the folder above". Docker's build engine, **BuildKit**, only receives the files the build actually uses, but a huge folder still slows builds down; a later lesson shows how to leave files out.

Useful options:

- `-f docker/Dockerfile.prod`: use a Dockerfile with another name or in another folder.
- `-t` can be repeated: `-t myapp:1.4.2 -t myapp:1.4 -t myapp:latest`.
- `--build-arg VERSION=1.4.2`: hand a value to the build; the Dockerfile picks it up with an `ARG VERSION` line.
- `--no-cache`: Docker normally reuses the results of steps it already ran in earlier builds; this makes every step run again.
- `--progress=plain`: print the full output of every step, handy when a `RUN` step fails and you need to see why.

**Naming versions** matters once images leave your laptop. Give every build a name that will never be reused, such as a version number (`1.4.2`) or the ID of the code change it was built from (`git-3f9a2c1`, from git, the tool most teams use to track code changes). You can also keep handy labels such as `1.4` or `latest` pointing at the newest build.

When you **deploy**, meaning put a version into service on the computers that run it for real (together called **production**), use that never-reused name. You always know exactly what's running, and you can go back to the previous version if something breaks.

`docker tag` adds names afterwards: `docker tag myapp:1.4.2 registry.example.com/team/myapp:1.4.2` prepares an image for uploading to a registry (covered later). Run the result like any image: `docker run myapp:1.4.2`.
concepts.code:
docker build -t myapp:dev .
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.prod \
  --build-arg VERSION=1.4.2 \
  -t myapp:1.4.2 -t myapp:git-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .   # also name it after the git change

docker image ls myapp
# myapp  1.4.2        5e1c0a7b9d2f  ...
# myapp  git-3f9a2c1  5e1c0a7b9d2f  ...   <- same image ID: two names, one image
docker run --rm myapp:1.4.2
docker build --no-cache --progress=plain -t myapp:debug .   # redo every step, show all output
takeaways: The trailing . is the build context; COPY can't reach outside it
-t can be repeated; tags are just names for one image
Deploy names that are never reused (version or code-change ID), not latest
pitfalls: Running docker build with . from a big folder, such as your whole user folder, making Docker look through thousands of unrelated files.

quiz.q: Your Dockerfile has COPY ../shared/lib ./lib. What happens with docker build . in the project folder?
options: It fails because the path is outside the build context
quiz.explain: The build only sees files inside the build context folder.

concepts.name: Layers and the build cache
concepts.summary: Each Dockerfile step makes a layer Docker can reuse; order the steps so slow installs aren't redone on every code change.
concepts.why: A well-ordered Dockerfile rebuilds in seconds instead of minutes, all day long.
concepts.body:
Each instruction that changes files (`RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`) produces a **layer**: the set of files it added, changed or deleted. The image is these layers piled up. Instructions such as `ENV` and `CMD` only change the image's settings, so they add no files.

When you rebuild, BuildKit checks each step against its **cache**: the results it kept from earlier builds. A step is reused if its instruction is unchanged *and*, for `COPY`/`ADD`, the copied files are unchanged. To tell, it compares each file's **checksum**, a short fingerprint calculated from the file's contents. The crucial rule: **once a step misses the cache, every step after it is rebuilt.**

So order instructions from least to most frequently changing. The standard approach first copies the files that list the app's **dependencies** (the packages it needs), installs them, and only then copies the rest of the code. For a Node.js app, `npm ci` is the install command, and `package-lock.json` lists the exact versions:

```dockerfile
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

Editing your code now changes only what the last `COPY` copies, so the slow `npm ci` step stays cached until `package-lock.json` changes. Copying everything first would reinstall every dependency on each code change.

Other layer facts that matter:

- Deleting a file in a later layer **does not shrink the image**; the earlier layer still contains it. Clean up in the same `RUN` that created the mess (`apt-get` is the package installer of Debian and Ubuntu, which many images are built on): `apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.
- `RUN apt-get update` (which fetches the list of available packages) alone in its own step is cached forever, so the list goes out of date; always chain it with the install.
- Docker judges a `RUN` step by its text, not by what's out on the internet, so `RUN curl .../latest.tar.gz` (a download) won't download again. Use `--no-cache`, or pass a changing value with `--build-arg`, when you need fresh content.

`docker image history <image>` shows each layer's size and the instruction that made it.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app

# 1. Rarely changes: cached unless the lockfile changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# 2. Changes on every commit: only this layer and below rebuild
COPY . .

# Install + clean up in ONE layer, or the cleanup saves nothing
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
takeaways: Each RUN/COPY/ADD creates a layer; once one step can't be reused, everything after it is rebuilt
Copy the dependency list and install before copying the rest of the code
Clean up in the same RUN; later deletions don't shrink earlier layers
Chain apt-get update with install in one RUN
pitfalls: COPY . . near the top of the Dockerfile, so every code edit reinstalls all dependencies.

quiz.q: You change one line in src/app.js. Which steps rebuild in the example Dockerfile?
options: COPY . . and every step after it
quiz.explain: The COPY . . step's file checksums changed, so it and everything after it miss the cache.

quiz.q: A RUN step downloads a 300 MB archive and a later RUN deletes it. How much does the deletion save in the final image?
options: Nothing; the earlier layer still contains the file
It depends on the base image
quiz.explain: Layers only add up; the deletion is saved in a new layer as a 'deleted' marker that hides the file.

concepts.name: Keeping the build context lean: .dockerignore
concepts.summary: List files to leave out of the build context in .dockerignore: builds get faster, reuse more, and stop leaking passwords and keys.
concepts.why: Without it, bulky folders and files full of passwords end up slowing builds or, worse, inside your image.
concepts.body:
The build context is everything in the directory you pass to `docker build`. A **`.dockerignore`** file in the root of the context lists the files to exclude, using wildcards, much like `.gitignore` does for git.

Why it matters:

- **Speed**: sending a 2 GB `node_modules` folder (where a Node.js project keeps its installed packages) or `.git` folder (git's history) to the builder wastes time on every build.
- **Reuse**: `COPY . .` fingerprints everything it copies. If `.git` or log files are included, the step can't be reused whenever they change, even when your code didn't.
- **Security**: files holding **secrets** (passwords, keys and other private values), such as `.env` settings files or the keys you use to log in to servers, get copied into the image by `COPY . .`, and anyone who pulls the image can read them.
- **Correctness**: copying your host's `node_modules`, with add-ons built for macOS, over the container's Linux ones causes confusing errors.

How to write it:

- One rule per line; `#` starts a comment.
- Paths are relative to the context root; `*` matches any characters within one folder or file name, `**` any number of folders deep.
- `!pattern` re-includes something excluded earlier, and the last matching line wins.
- Some teams invert it: start with `*`, then allow only what's needed with `!src` and `!package*.json`.

The file must sit at the **root of the build context**, not necessarily next to the Dockerfile. With BuildKit you can also give a Dockerfile its own ignore file by naming it after it, for example `Dockerfile.prod.dockerignore`.
concepts.code:
# .dockerignore
.git
.gitignore
**/node_modules
**/__pycache__
*.log
dist/
coverage/

# secrets and local config
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
**/*.pem

# not needed inside the image
Dockerfile*
compose*.yaml
README.md
takeaways: .dockerignore excludes files from the build context
It speeds up builds, lets steps be reused and keeps secrets out
It must be at the context root; ! re-includes; last match wins
pitfalls: Relying on .gitignore — Docker ignores it; only .dockerignore affects the build context.

quiz.q: Your build cache keeps busting on COPY . . even though source files didn't change. What is a likely cause?
options: The base image is too old
Files like .git or logs are in the context and change on every commit
quiz.explain: COPY fingerprints everything it copies, so files that change all the time stop it being reused unless they're ignored.

concepts.name: Multi-stage builds
concepts.summary: Use several FROM stages: build your program with all the heavy tools, then ship only the finished result in a small final image.
concepts.why: It's the single most effective way to make production images small and secure.
concepts.body:
Building software often needs heavy tools: a **compiler** (a program that turns code into a ready-to-run program), test tools, download caches. Running it needs none of that.

A **multi-stage build** puts several `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile. Each starts a new **build stage**, and you copy just the files you want from an earlier stage with `COPY --from=<stage>`. Only the **last stage** becomes the image (unless you pick another), so the build tools never reach production.

Typical shapes:

- **Compiled languages** such as Go and Rust, whose compiler outputs one ready-to-run program file (a **binary**): build in `golang:1.25`, then copy just the binary into `gcr.io/distroless/static` (a tiny image with almost nothing in it) or even `scratch` (a completely empty one). The image shrinks from about 1 GB to about 10 MB.
- **Websites**: `npm run build` in a Node.js stage produces the finished web pages; copy the `dist/` folder into an `nginx` stage that serves them.
- **Python or Node.js apps**: install dependencies in a stage that has build tools (some packages must be compiled while installing), then copy the installed packages into a slim final stage.

Name stages with `AS`, as in `FROM golang:1.25 AS build`, and refer to them by name.

Other useful tricks:

- `docker build --target test .` stops at the named stage, so one Dockerfile can define dev, test and prod images.
- `COPY --from=nginx:1.27 /etc/nginx/nginx.conf .` copies from any image, not just stages.
- BuildKit builds stages that don't depend on each other **at the same time**, and skips stages the target doesn't need.

Make sure the final stage has everything the program needs while running: the files used to check secure web connections, time zone data, and the system library most Linux programs rely on (the C library). A Go binary built with `CGO_ENABLED=0` doesn't need that library, so it runs even in `scratch`.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/server ./cmd/server

FROM build AS test
RUN go test ./...

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 AS prod
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

# docker build -t api:prod .              -> last stage (prod), ~10 MB
# docker build --target test -t api:test .
takeaways: Only the final (or --target) stage becomes the image
COPY --from=stage copies artifacts between stages
--target lets one Dockerfile produce dev, test and prod images
Check the final stage has the security files, system library and data the app needs
pitfalls: Copying a binary that needs the C library into scratch or distroless/static, where it fails with a confusing 'no such file or directory'.

quiz.q: In a multi-stage Dockerfile without --target, which stage becomes the image?
quiz.explain: The final stage is the default target; earlier stages exist only to feed it.

quiz.q: What does COPY --from=build /out/app /app do?
options: Copies /out/app from the stage named build into the current stage
quiz.explain: --from takes files from an earlier stage (or any image) instead of the build context.

concepts.name: Persisting data with volumes
concepts.summary: Store data outside a container's writable layer in Docker-managed named volumes that survive container removal.
concepts.why: Databases and uploads must outlive containers, which are meant to be disposable.
concepts.body:
A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed, and writing heavily to it is slow. For data that must be kept, such as the files of a **database** (a program that stores and organises an app's data), use a **Docker volume**: storage managed by Docker, living outside any container, attached at a folder inside it.

```bash
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17
```

Remove and recreate the `db` container (to upgrade the image, say) with the same `-v pgdata:...` and the data is still there.

The longer `--mount` form says the same thing and is easier to read in commands you save in files: `--mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data`.

Things to know:

- If you mount a volume that doesn't exist, Docker creates it.
- When an **empty** volume is mounted over a directory that has content in the image, Docker copies that content into the volume first. Handy for seeding config.
- `-v /data` with no name creates an **anonymous volume** with a random ID. They're removed along with the container if you used `--rm` (or `docker rm -v`); otherwise they linger.
- Volumes can be shared by several containers at once; append `:ro` to mount read-only.
- `docker volume ls`, `inspect`, `rm` and `prune` manage them. Removing containers never removes named volumes, which is good for data and bad for disk space.

To back up a volume, attach it to a throwaway container together with a host folder, and pack its files into one archive file with `tar`. That works the same everywhere, including Docker Desktop, where volume files live inside the VM rather than on your Mac or PC.
concepts.code:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev \
  --mount type=volume,src=pgdata,dst=/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17

docker rm -f db                  # container gone...
docker run -d --name db -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17   # ...data still there

# Back up the volume to ./pgdata.tgz
docker run --rm -v pgdata:/data:ro -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/pgdata.tgz -C /data .

docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata --format '{{.Mountpoint}}'
takeaways: Volumes are Docker-managed storage that outlives containers
`-v name:/path` or `--mount type=volume,src=...,dst=...`
Empty volumes are pre-filled from the image's content at that path
Back up with a throwaway container that tars the volume
pitfalls: Running a database without a volume, then losing all data on docker rm.

quiz.q: You run docker rm -f db on a container using named volume pgdata. What happens to pgdata?
options: It is deleted with the container
It is kept until you remove it explicitly
It is converted to an image layer
quiz.explain: Named volumes have their own lifecycle independent of containers.

quiz.q: An empty new volume is mounted at /etc/app, where the image has default config files. What does the container see?
options: The image's files, copied into the volume first
A merged view that isn't saved
quiz.explain: Docker populates an empty named volume with the image's content at the mount point.

concepts.name: Bind mounts and tmpfs
concepts.summary: Show a host folder inside a container for live editing, or give it a memory-only tmpfs folder for scratch files.
concepts.why: Bind mounts let you edit code on your computer and see the app in the container update at once; knowing their pitfalls saves hours.
concepts.body:
A **bind mount** maps an existing path on the host directly into the container. Unlike a volume, Docker doesn't manage it; the container sees your real files, and changes go both ways instantly.

```bash
docker run -v "$PWD":/app -w /app node:22 npm run dev
```

That's the classic development setup: you edit files on the host, and the app's development mode inside the container notices and reloads. The `--mount` form is `--mount type=bind,src="$PWD",dst=/app`; unlike `-v`, it errors if the source path doesn't exist instead of creating an empty directory, which catches typos.

Key behaviours and gotchas:

- A bind mount **hides** whatever the image had at that path. Mounting your project over `/app` also hides the `node_modules` installed in the image. A common fix is an extra anonymous volume for that subfolder: `-v /app/node_modules`.
- **Permissions**: Linux stores each file's owner as a number, the user ID. A container running as the administrator (root) creates files in your project that only the administrator can change; a container running as another user may be unable to write your files. On Linux, run with `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"` to use your own user ID.
- **Speed**: on Docker Desktop, bind-mounted files are slower than on Linux, because every file access crosses into the hidden VM; for heavy file use, Docker Desktop's file-sharing speed-ups or volumes help.
- Append `:ro` (or `readonly` with `--mount`) for settings files the container should only read.
- Bind mounts tie a container to the host's directory layout, so use them for development and for specific host files, and use volumes for application data.

A **tmpfs mount** (`--tmpfs /tmp`) is a folder kept only in memory, which vanishes when the container stops. Use it for scratch files and for secrets that must never be written to disk. It pairs well with `--read-only`, which stops the container writing anywhere else.
concepts.code:
# Live-reload dev server, keeping the image's node_modules
docker run --rm -it -p 5173:5173 \
  -v "$PWD":/app -v /app/node_modules -w /app \
  node:22 npm run dev -- --host

# Read-only config file from the host
docker run -d --name proxy \
  --mount type=bind,src="$PWD"/nginx.conf,dst=/etc/nginx/nginx.conf,readonly \
  -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27

# Avoid root-owned files in your project (Linux)
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" alpine touch out.txt

# In-memory scratch space on a read-only container
docker run --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp alpine sh -c 'echo hi > /tmp/x && cat /tmp/x'
takeaways: Bind mounts expose a host path directly; changes are live both ways
They hide the image's content at the mount point
Watch file owners' user IDs, and file speed on Docker Desktop
tmpfs mounts are in-memory and disappear on stop
pitfalls: Mounting the project over /app and wondering where node_modules went.

quiz.q: You bind-mount your project to /app, but the image installed dependencies in /app/node_modules. What does the container see?
options: Your host's /app contents only; the image's node_modules is hidden
quiz.explain: A mount replaces the view of the directory underneath it.

quiz.q: Which mount type should hold a production database's data?
options: A bind mount to the project folder
quiz.explain: Volumes are managed by Docker, portable across hosts and suited to persistent app data.

concepts.name: Publishing ports
concepts.summary: Make an app in a container reachable from outside with -p host:container, and choose who outside can reach it.
concepts.why: Nothing inside a container is reachable from your browser until you publish its port.
concepts.body:
Each container gets its own private network, with its own **IP address** (the numeric address computers use to find each other on a network, like 172.17.0.2). So an app listening on port 80 inside a container is not reachable from the host or the outside world until you **publish** the port:

```bash
docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
```

The format is `-p [host_ip:]host_port:container_port[/protocol]`. Here, host port 8080 forwards to container port 80, so `http://localhost:8080` reaches nginx (**localhost** is your computer's name for itself).

Details that matter:

- By default the port is opened on **every network connection** the host has (written `0.0.0.0`), so other computers on your network can reach it, not just you. On Linux, Docker's own network rules even slip past the host's **firewall** (the software that stops unwanted connections, such as ufw). For anything only you should reach, use `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80`; `127.0.0.1` is localhost's numeric address.
- Two containers can't publish the same host port. Pick different host ports (`8081:80`, `8082:80`), or put one front-door program in front that passes each request to the right container (a **reverse proxy**).
- `-p 80` (no host port) picks a random free host port; `docker port web` shows the mapping.
- `-P` publishes every port the image `EXPOSE`s to random host ports. `EXPOSE` alone publishes nothing.
- Some apps use UDP, a second kind of network traffic; publish those with `/udp`: `-p 5353:53/udp`.

The app inside must listen on `0.0.0.0` (every connection), not `127.0.0.1`. Inside a container, `127.0.0.1` means the container itself, and published traffic doesn't arrive there. Many tools for building web apps listen only on `127.0.0.1` by default during development, so this is the number one cause of "the port is published but the connection is refused".

Containers talking to each other don't need published ports at all; they use a shared network, covered next.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
curl -s localhost:8080 | head -1          # <!DOCTYPE html>

docker run -d --name admin -p 127.0.0.1:9000:80 nginx:1.27   # local only
docker run -d --name rand -p 80 nginx:1.27
docker port rand                          # 80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:49154

# App must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 python:3.13 \
  python -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0
takeaways: -p host:container publishes a port; EXPOSE is documentation only
By default the whole network can connect; use 127.0.0.1: to allow only your own computer
The app must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
Container-to-container traffic doesn't need published ports
pitfalls: Publishing a database with -p 5432:5432 on a cloud VM and exposing it to the internet despite the firewall.

quiz.q: The port is published with -p 3000:3000 but the browser gets 'connection refused'. The app logs 'listening on 127.0.0.1:3000'. Fix?
quiz.explain: Published traffic arrives on the container's network connection, not on its private 127.0.0.1 address.

quiz.q: What does EXPOSE 8080 in a Dockerfile do by itself?
options: Documents the port and lets -P publish it
quiz.explain: EXPOSE is metadata; publishing requires -p or -P at run time.

concepts.name: Container networking
concepts.summary: Put containers on a network you create, so they can reach each other by name.
concepts.why: Apps made of several containers (say, a website plus its database) depend on them finding each other reliably.
concepts.body:
Docker offers several kinds of network:

- **bridge**: a private virtual network on one host. The default for containers.
- **host**: the container uses the host's network directly, with no walls and no port publishing. Linux only, and occasionally used for speed.
- **none**: no networking at all.
- **overlay**, **macvlan** and **ipvlan**: special kinds for networks that span several hosts (with Docker Swarm) or that give containers their own addresses on your office network.

A **bridge network** is a private network inside one host. Containers started without `--network` join the **default bridge**, where they can reach each other only by IP address. Don't use it for apps. Create your own **user-defined bridge network** instead:

```bash
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet myapi
```

On a network you created, Docker runs a built-in name lookup, its **DNS** (the same kind of system that turns website names into IP addresses). It translates container names, and extra names set with `--network-alias`, into their current IP addresses, so `api` can connect to `postgres://db:5432`: the database `db`, on port 5432. IPs change when containers are recreated; names don't. Networks also isolate: containers on different networks can't talk unless one is attached to both (`docker network connect`).

Notice there's no `-p` on the database: container-to-container traffic flows over the network on the container's real port. Publish only what the outside world needs, such as the web app itself or a reverse proxy.

Reaching the host from a container: Docker Desktop provides `host.docker.internal`; on Linux add `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`.

`docker network inspect appnet` lists connected containers and their IPs. Docker Compose creates a network per project automatically, which is why services there can reach each other by service name.
concepts.code:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --name db --network appnet -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev postgres:17
docker run -d --name api --network appnet -p 8000:8000 \
  -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres myapi:1.0

# Name resolution from inside the network
docker run --rm --network appnet alpine nslookup db
# Name: db  Address: 172.18.0.2

docker network inspect appnet --format '{{range .Containers}}{{.Name}} {{end}}'
# db api

# Reach a service running on the host (Linux)
docker run --rm --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway alpine \
  ping -c1 host.docker.internal
takeaways: Create your own bridge networks; the default bridge can't look containers up by name
Containers on the same network reach each other by name on container ports
Only publish ports for traffic from outside Docker
host.docker.internal reaches the host (host-gateway on Linux)
pitfalls: Hard-coding container IP addresses — they change whenever containers are recreated.

quiz.q: api and db are both on user-defined network appnet; db has no -p flag. Can api connect to db:5432?
options: Yes, via Docker's DNS on the shared network
quiz.explain: Containers on the same network talk directly; publishing is only for the host/outside.

quiz.q: Two containers on the default bridge network try to reach each other by name. What happens?
options: It works the same as on user-defined networks
Name resolution fails; the default bridge has no automatic DNS for names
quiz.explain: Automatic name resolution is a feature of user-defined networks.

concepts.name: Environment variables and configuration
concepts.summary: Give one image different settings wherever it runs, with environment variables, settings files and mounted files, and know ARG from ENV.
concepts.why: One image should run on your laptop, in testing and in production; the settings are what change between them.
concepts.body:
Build an image once, then give it its settings each time a container starts. A widely followed rule of thumb (from the 'twelve-factor app' guidelines) says settings belong in the environment, not in the image.

Ways to pass configuration:

- `-e LOG_LEVEL=debug`: one environment variable. `-e API_KEY` with no value copies `API_KEY`'s value from your own terminal.
- `--env-file prod.env`: many `KEY=value` lines from a file.
- **Settings files**, such as `nginx.conf`, attached with a bind mount or volume (see the storage lessons).
- **Secrets** (passwords, keys and other private values) as files: tools that run many containers for you, such as Docker Compose and Kubernetes, can hand secrets to a container as files, and many official images accept a file name instead of a value, such as `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`.

In the Dockerfile there are two variable instructions, often confused:

- **`ARG`** exists only **during the build**. Set it with `--build-arg`. Useful for versions: `ARG NODE_VERSION=22` then `FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}`. An `ARG` written before `FROM` must be repeated inside the stage to be used there.
- **`ENV`** is set during the build **and** stays in every container as a default, which `-e` can replace.

Neither is a safe place for secrets. Both are recorded in the image (`docker history` and `docker inspect` reveal them), and environment variables of a running container are visible to anyone with access to `docker inspect`. Use BuildKit's secret mounts while building (a later lesson) and secret files when containers run.

Make your app read its config from the environment with sane defaults, and fail fast with a clear message when a required variable is missing.
concepts.code:
# Dockerfile excerpt
#   ARG APP_VERSION=dev          # build time only
#   ENV PORT=8000 LOG_LEVEL=info # defaults for every container
#   LABEL version=$APP_VERSION

docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.4.2 -t api:1.4.2 .

cat > prod.env <<'END'
LOG_LEVEL=warn
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app@db:5432/app
END
docker run -d --env-file prod.env -e PORT=9000 -p 9000:9000 api:1.4.2
docker exec $(docker ps -lq) printenv LOG_LEVEL PORT    # warn / 9000

docker inspect --format '{{json .Config.Env}}' api:1.4.2   # ENV is visible!
takeaways: Build once, give settings when containers start with -e, --env-file and mounted files
ARG = build time only; ENV = build time and container default
ARG and ENV values can be read from the image's details: never put secrets there
pitfalls: Baking a real password into the image with ENV: anyone who can pull the image can read it.

quiz.q: Which Dockerfile instruction's value is NOT available to the running container?
quiz.explain: ARG exists only during the build (unless copied into an ENV).

quiz.q: Why shouldn't secrets be passed as build args?
options: Build args are limited to 64 characters
They're recorded in image metadata and history
quiz.explain: Build args used in steps appear in the image history; use BuildKit secret mounts.

concepts.name: Docker Compose
concepts.summary: Define a multi-container app (services, networks, volumes) in compose.yaml and run it with docker compose up.
concepts.why: Compose turns a page of docker run commands into one versioned file that the whole team runs the same way.
concepts.body:
Real apps are often several containers: the web app, its database, a program doing background jobs. **Docker Compose** lets you describe them all in one file, `compose.yaml`, and manage them together as one project with the `docker compose` command. You write down what should be running; Compose works out the steps.

The file is written in **YAML**, a simple text format of `name: value` lines in which indenting a line puts it inside the line above.

The file's top-level keys:

- `services`: each service is a container definition, with `image` or `build`, `ports`, `environment`, `env_file`, `volumes`, `depends_on`, `command` and so on, mirroring `docker run` flags.
- `volumes`: named volumes the services use.
- `networks`: optional; by default Compose creates one network for the project, and every service can reach every other **by service name**.

The old top-level `version:` key is obsolete and ignored.

Core commands, run in the folder with the file:

- `docker compose up -d`: build or pull as needed, create the network and volumes, start everything in the background. Run it again after editing the file and only changed services are recreated.
- `docker compose ps`, `logs -f api`, `exec db psql -U postgres`.
- `docker compose up -d --build`: rebuild images first.
- `docker compose down`: stop and remove containers and the network. Volumes are kept unless you add `-v`.

Compose fills in placeholders like `${TAG:-latest}` (the value of `TAG`, or `latest` if it isn't set) from your terminal session's environment or from a `.env` file next to `compose.yaml`. That `.env` file only **fills in the placeholders in the file**; `env_file:` passes environment variables **into containers**. They are different mechanisms.

`depends_on` controls start **order** only; by default it doesn't wait for the database to be ready. Combine it with health checks (`condition: service_healthy`), covered later, or make the app keep trying to connect.
concepts.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    image: acme/api:${TAG:-dev}
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8000:8000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      - db
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  pgdata:
# docker compose up -d --build ; docker compose logs -f api ; docker compose down
takeaways: compose.yaml lists the services, volumes and networks of one project
Services reach each other by service name on the project network
Running up -d again only recreates what changed; down keeps volumes unless -v
.env fills in placeholders in the file; env_file passes environment variables into containers
pitfalls: Assuming depends_on waits until the database accepts connections — it only orders startup unless you use a health condition.

quiz.q: How does the api service connect to the db service in the same compose project?
options: Via the db service name, e.g. db:5432
Only via a published host port
It needs a manual docker network connect
quiz.explain: Compose puts services on a shared project network with DNS for service names.

quiz.q: What does docker compose down do to named volumes by default?
quiz.explain: Volumes survive down; add -v to remove them.

concepts.name: Registries: pushing and pulling images
concepts.summary: Upload images to Docker Hub or a private registry, log in with docker login, and refer to exact images by digest.
concepts.why: Registries are how images get from your build to servers, automated build systems and teammates.
concepts.body:
A **registry** stores and serves images. Docker Hub (`docker.io`) is the default; others include registries run by code-hosting sites (such as `ghcr.io`), by cloud companies (Amazon ECR, Google's and Azure's registries) and ones you run yourself, such as Harbor.

The image name says where it goes: `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2` means registry `ghcr.io`, image name `acme/api`, tag `1.4.2`. To push, the local image must carry that name:

```bash
docker login ghcr.io
docker tag api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
```

Pushes and pulls are layer-based: layers the registry already has, such as your base image's layers, aren't uploaded again.

**Logging in**: `docker login` saves your login details with a **credential helper** (a program that keeps them in your operating system's secure password store) or, failing that, in the plain file `~/.docker/config.json`. Log in with an **access token** (a password-like code you create for one purpose and can cancel at any time) rather than your real password. In **CI** (automated systems that build and test every code change), use tokens that expire quickly.

**Tags vs digests**: a tag can be changed; someone can push a different image under `1.4.2` tomorrow. The **digest** (`ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:...`), printed after each push, is calculated from the image's contents and can never change. When production must run exactly the image you tested, refer to it by digest; tools such as Renovate keep those references up to date.

**Docker Hub limits**: Docker Hub caps how many pulls per hour it allows without logging in, or on free accounts. CI systems that pull a lot should log in, use a mirror (a nearby registry that keeps copies of images it has already fetched), or pull base images from another registry.

Private repositories require `docker login` on every machine that pulls them, including servers and CI runners.
concepts.code:
echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u my-user --password-stdin
docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 -t ghcr.io/acme/api:latest .
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
# 1.4.2: digest: sha256:7c3e...a1f9 size: 1784
docker push ghcr.io/acme/api:latest       # layers already exist: instant

# Pull an exact, immutable image
docker pull ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:7c3e...a1f9
docker image inspect ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}'
docker logout ghcr.io
takeaways: The registry host is part of the image name; tag images to match before pushing
Push/pull transfer only missing layers
Tags can be changed; digests never change
Log CI in to avoid Docker Hub's pull limits
pitfalls: Typing a password after -p in the command itself, where it's saved in your terminal's command history: use --password-stdin.

quiz.q: You push api:1.4.2 to a registry, and later a colleague pushes a different build with the same tag. Which reference still gets your original image?
quiz.explain: Digests identify content immutably; tags can be repointed.

concepts.name: Small and secure images
concepts.summary: Make images smaller and safer: minimal base images, no administrator user, exact versions, no secrets, and scanning for known security holes.
concepts.why: Every package in an image is one more thing an attacker could exploit and one more thing to download; production images should carry only what the app needs to run.
concepts.body:
Image size and security improve together: fewer packages means fewer **vulnerabilities** (known security holes in software), smaller downloads and faster start-up on new servers.

**Choose a minimal base.** Roughly from largest to smallest:

- Full images (`python:3.13`, `node:22`): convenient, but hundreds of megabytes and many packages.
- `-slim` versions: Debian (a Linux version) with the extras removed. A good default for Python or Node.js apps.
- `alpine`: tiny, but built on a different C library (musl, the basic system library programs rely on) from most Linux versions, so some ready-made binaries and Python packages break or run slower. Test before switching.
- **Distroless images** (`gcr.io/distroless/...`) and similar hardened ones: only what's needed to run the app, with no shell and no package installer.
- `scratch`: completely empty, for binaries that need nothing else.

Combine with multi-stage builds so compilers never reach the final image.

**Don't run as root.** Add a user and switch with `USER 10001`. A numeric user ID works everywhere, including Kubernetes (a popular system for running containers across many servers), which can check that a container doesn't run as root. Root, the administrator, inside a container is held back, but it still makes a break-out from the container, or a simple mistake, far more damaging.

**Keep secrets out.** Not in `COPY`, `ARG` or `ENV`; use `.dockerignore`, BuildKit secret mounts and secrets handed over when the container starts. Anything in any layer can be extracted, even if a later layer deletes it.

**Fix versions and update.** Name exact base image versions (or digests) so builds are repeatable, and rebuild regularly so operating system security fixes reach your image. Tools such as Dependabot or Renovate automate both.

**Scan and document.** `docker scout cves <image>` (or Trivy, Grype) lists the known vulnerabilities in each package. `docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true` attaches an **SBOM** (a list of every package and version in the image) and a signed note of how the image was built.

When running, add `--read-only` (no writing outside volumes), `--cap-drop ALL` and `--security-opt no-new-privileges` (both remove administrator powers; see the Expert lessons) where the app allows.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim AS build
RUN python -m venv /venv
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN /venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.13-slim
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin app
COPY --from=build /venv /venv
COPY --chown=10001:10001 src/ /app/
WORKDIR /app
USER 10001
ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]

# docker scout cves api:1.4.2
# docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL api:1.4.2
takeaways: Smaller base = fewer vulnerabilities and faster pulls; test alpine before adopting it
Run as a numeric non-root USER
Secrets in any layer are recoverable: keep them out of the build
Use exact versions, rebuild often, scan with docker scout or Trivy
pitfalls: Switching to alpine for size, then finding Python or Node.js packages that are slow or broken on its different C library.

quiz.q: Why is a distroless image harder to attack than a full distro image?
options: It contains no shell or package manager and far fewer packages
quiz.explain: Less software means fewer vulnerabilities and fewer tools for an attacker to use.

quiz.q: A Dockerfile COPYs id_rsa, uses it in a RUN, then deletes it in the next RUN. Is the key in the image?
options: Only if the image is pushed
Yes, the earlier layer still contains it
quiz.explain: Layers are immutable; deletion in a later layer doesn't remove the data from earlier ones.

concepts.name: Healthchecks and restart policies
concepts.summary: Tell Docker how to test that your app works with HEALTHCHECK, and how to recover from crashes with restart policies.
concepts.why: A running process isn't necessarily a working service; health and restart settings close that gap.
concepts.body:
Docker only knows whether the main process is running. A website program that has frozen, stuck forever waiting, is still "Up". A **health check** (`HEALTHCHECK`) gives Docker a command that tests whether the app really works:

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/healthz || exit 1
```

Docker runs the command inside the container on that schedule. Exit code 0 means healthy, 1 unhealthy. The status changes from `starting` to `healthy`, or to `unhealthy` after `retries` consecutive failures, and shows in `docker ps` and `docker inspect`. `--start-period` gives slow starters time before failures count. The check needs its tool (curl, wget or a small purpose-built program) inside the image, which matters for minimal images that contain almost nothing. You can also set or replace it when starting a container (`--health-cmd`) or in Compose (`healthcheck:`).

What uses health status: Compose's `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` waits for it, Docker Swarm replaces unhealthy containers, and **monitoring** tools (which watch your systems and alert people) can warn on it. Plain `docker run` does **not** restart an unhealthy container by itself. (Kubernetes, a popular system for running containers across many servers, ignores Docker health checks and uses its own.)

**Restart policies** (`--restart`) handle crashes and computer restarts:

- `no` (default): never restart.
- `on-failure[:5]`: restart only on a non-zero exit, optionally at most 5 times.
- `always`: restart whenever it stops; a container you stopped manually comes back when the daemon restarts.
