- `unless-stopped`: like `always`, but a manual `docker stop` is respected across daemon restarts.

Docker waits progressively longer between restarts of a crash-looping container. For servers, `unless-stopped` with a healthcheck is a sensible single-host baseline.
concepts.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4.2
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
# docker compose ps  ->  db  Up 20 seconds (healthy)
takeaways: HEALTHCHECK runs a command in the container: 0 healthy, 1 unhealthy
Plain Docker reports unhealthy but doesn't restart it; Compose and Swarm can act on it
Restart policies: no, on-failure, always, unless-stopped
depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for readiness
pitfalls: Using a healthcheck command (like curl) that isn't installed in the image, so the container is always unhealthy.

quiz.q: A container's healthcheck reports unhealthy and it runs with --restart always. What does Docker do?
options: Keeps it running and reports it as unhealthy
quiz.explain: Restart policies react to the process exiting, not to health status.

quiz.q: Which restart policy keeps a container you stopped manually from coming back after a daemon restart?
quiz.explain: unless-stopped respects a manual stop; always restarts it when the daemon starts.

concepts.name: Resource limits
concepts.summary: Cap a container's memory, CPU and number of processes, and recognise when it's killed for using too much memory.
concepts.why: Without limits, one leaky container can starve every other service on the host.
concepts.body:
By default a container may use all of the host's CPU and memory. The kernel enforces limits through a feature called control groups (cgroups, covered in the Expert lessons), and you set them on `docker run` (or in Compose):

- `--memory 512m`: hard memory limit. If the container goes over it, the kernel's **out-of-memory (OOM) killer** ends a process in it, usually the main one, and the container exits with code **137**. `docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'` confirms it.
- `--memory-swap`: memory plus **swap** (disk space the system uses as slow extra memory). Setting it equal to `--memory` gives the container no swap.
- `--memory-reservation`: a soft limit applied when the host is under memory pressure.
- `--cpus 1.5`: at most 1.5 CPUs' worth of time. Going over it makes the container **slower**, not killed.
- `--cpu-shares`: a relative weight that only matters when CPUs are contended.
- `--cpuset-cpus 0,1`: run only on cores 0 and 1 (a CPU has several cores, each running one thing at a time).
- `--pids-limit 200`: cap the number of processes, which stops a program that keeps copying itself from swamping the host.

`docker stats` shows live usage against limits. `docker update --memory 1g api` changes limits on a running container.

Make the program that runs your code **aware of its limits**. Modern Java and Go read the container's limits by themselves, though Go only started doing so for CPU (`GOMAXPROCS`) in recent versions. Recent Node.js versions size their memory use from the container's limit too, but the `--max-old-space-size` setting is still common. Many apps start one helper process per CPU they see, which means the host's CPUs, not your limit, so set those counts yourself.

In Compose, use `deploy.resources.limits` (`cpus`, `memory`) and optionally `reservations`; `docker compose up` applies them.

Set limits from measurements: watch real usage under load, then add headroom. A limit that's too tight produces mysterious exit 137 restarts.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api --memory 512m --memory-swap 512m \
  --cpus 1.5 --pids-limit 200 acme/api:1.4.2

docker stats --no-stream api
# NAME  CPU %   MEM USAGE / LIMIT    MEM %   PIDS
# api   37.2%   311MiB / 512MiB      60.7%   23

docker inspect api --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} OOM={{.State.OOMKilled}}'
# 137 OOM=true   (after a memory spike)

docker update --memory 1g --memory-swap 1g api

# compose.yaml equivalent:
#   deploy:
#     resources:
#       limits: { cpus: "1.5", memory: 512M }
takeaways: Default is unlimited; set --memory, --cpus and --pids-limit for production
Memory over the limit = OOM kill (exit 137); CPU over the limit = slowed down
Make Java, Node.js and per-CPU helper counts aware of the limits
pitfalls: Setting a memory limit without telling Java, Node.js or the app's helper processes, so the app is killed again and again for using too much memory.

quiz.q: A container exceeds its --cpus 1 limit under load. What happens?
options: It is throttled and runs slower
quiz.explain: CPU limits are enforced by throttling; only memory overuse leads to kills.

quiz.q: A container keeps exiting with code 137 and OOMKilled=true. What does that indicate?
options: A crash in the app's own code
It exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
quiz.explain: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); OOMKilled confirms the memory limit was hit.

concepts.name: BuildKit features
concepts.summary: Use BuildKit's cache mounts, secret mounts and shared build cache to make builds faster and keep secrets out of images.
concepts.why: These features cut build times on CI machines dramatically and are the right way to use secrets during builds.
concepts.body:
**BuildKit** is Docker's build engine (the default since Engine 23; `docker build` is shorthand for `docker buildx build`). Beyond building stages at the same time and skipping unused ones, it adds Dockerfile features. Start the file with `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1` to always get the newest stable set of them.

**Cache mounts** keep a folder between builds without putting it in the image:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Even when the step itself can't be reused, package installers such as `pip`, `npm` or `apt` find their earlier downloads still there, so reinstalls take seconds.

**Secret mounts** lend a secret file to a single `RUN` without writing it into any layer or the build history:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
```

and build with `docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc .`.

**SSH mounts** (`RUN --mount=type=ssh git clone git@github.com:acme/private.git` with `docker build --ssh default .`) let one step use your **SSH** login (the key-based way to log in to servers and private code repositories) to download private code, without copying your key into the image.

**Bind mounts** here (`--mount=type=bind,source=.,target=/src`) let one step read files from the build context without copying them into a layer, useful when only the step's output should end up in the image.

Writing `RUN <<EOF`, then several lines of commands, then `EOF` on a line of its own, puts a whole small script inside one `RUN`.

**Shared cache**: CI machines usually start every build with an empty cache. `--cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/api:buildcache,mode=max` uploads the cache of every layer to a registry, and `--cache-from` with the same name downloads it on the next run (`type=gha` does the same with one popular CI service's storage). Uploading cache to a registry needs a builder made with `docker buildx create --driver docker-container`, or Docker's newer containerd image store.

`docker buildx du` and `docker buildx prune` manage the builder's cache.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/var/cache/apt,sharing=locked \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/var/lib/apt,sharing=locked \
    rm -f /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/docker-clean && \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=requirements.txt \
    --mount=type=secret,id=pipconf,target=/etc/pip.conf \
    pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "main.py"]

# docker build --secret id=pipconf,src=$HOME/.config/pip/pip.conf \
#   --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/app:cache \
#   --cache-to type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/app:cache,mode=max -t app .
takeaways: RUN --mount=type=cache keeps installers' downloads between builds
Secret and SSH mounts give a single step access without leaking into layers
Upload the cache to a registry so CI builds don't start from scratch
Begin Dockerfiles with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
pitfalls: Expecting a cache mount's contents to be in the final image — they're only available during that RUN.

quiz.q: How does a BuildKit secret mount differ from COPY-ing a token file?
options: The secret is available only during that RUN and is never stored in a layer
It works only with Docker Hub
quiz.explain: Secret mounts are ephemeral, so the image and history never contain the secret.

quiz.q: Your CI builds always start cold. Which feature helps most?
options: --cache-to/--cache-from with a registry or gha cache
quiz.explain: Exporting and importing build cache lets fresh runners reuse previous layers.

concepts.name: Multi-platform builds
concepts.summary: Build one image name for both Intel/AMD (amd64) and arm64 processors, by imitating the other processor or by faster cross-compiling.
concepts.why: Apple Silicon laptops, Graviton servers and Raspberry Pis all need arm64 images alongside amd64.
concepts.body:
Processors come in families that understand different machine instructions, called **CPU architectures**. Most PCs and servers use amd64 (Intel and AMD); Apple Silicon Macs, many cloud servers and Raspberry Pis use arm64. An image built on an amd64 machine contains amd64 binaries, which won't run directly on arm64, and vice versa.

A **multi-platform image** is one tag that points to an **image index**: a list with a separate image per platform. Each computer automatically pulls the one it can run.

Build one with buildx:

```bash
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --push .
```

Docker's classic local image storage can't hold multi-platform images, so you either `--push` straight to a registry or turn on the newer **containerd image store** (the default in recent Docker Desktop installs), which can. A builder made with `docker buildx create --driver docker-container --use` also works.

There are two ways to produce foreign-architecture binaries:

- **Emulation**: **QEMU**, a program that imitates another processor in software, lets BuildKit run arm64 `RUN` steps on an amd64 machine. Docker Desktop includes it; on Linux install it with `docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install all`. It's simple but can be 5 to 20 times slower for compile-heavy steps.
- **Cross-compilation**: run the build stage on the builder's own platform at full speed, and tell the compiler which platform to produce a program for. BuildKit fills in `BUILDPLATFORM`, `TARGETPLATFORM`, `TARGETOS` and `TARGETARCH` automatically as `ARG` values:

```dockerfile
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.25 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
RUN GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /app .
```

Go, Rust and Zig cross-compile easily, and Node.js or Python apps without compiled add-ons don't need compiling at all.

A third option is a real machine of each architecture doing its share of the build (`docker buildx create --append`), or arm64 CI machines. Check the result with `docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>`.
concepts.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang:1.25 AS build
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH go build -o /out/api ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

# docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
#   -t ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2 --push .
# docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.2
#   Platform: linux/amd64 ... Platform: linux/arm64
takeaways: One tag, one image index, one image per platform
--platform a,b with --push (or the containerd image store to load locally)
Emulation is easy but slow; cross-compile with FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM
TARGETOS/TARGETARCH are provided automatically
pitfalls: Running every compile step under QEMU emulation and accepting 30-minute builds that cross-compilation would cut to minutes.

quiz.q: What does FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM achieve in a cross-compiling stage?
options: Forces the final image to the build machine's architecture
Runs the build stage natively on the builder, avoiding emulation
quiz.explain: The compiler runs natively and targets TARGETOS/TARGETARCH, so no QEMU is needed for that stage.

quiz.q: A user on an arm64 laptop runs docker pull of a multi-platform tag. What do they get?
options: The arm64 image, chosen from the index
quiz.explain: The client selects the matching platform entry from the image index.

concepts.name: Debugging containers
concepts.summary: Find out why containers crash, can't connect or have no shell, using logs, inspect, events, exit codes and separate tool containers.
concepts.why: Containers fail in container-specific ways, and minimal images strip out the usual tools.
concepts.body:
Work from the outside in.

**Why did it stop?** `docker ps -a` shows the exit code, and `docker logs` shows the last output. Common codes: `0`, the process simply finished (often a command that should have kept running); `1`, the app reported an error; `126`, the command exists but isn't allowed to run; `127`, command not found (a wrong `CMD`, a script file saved on Windows with the wrong invisible end-of-line characters, or a script whose language, such as Python, isn't installed in the image); `137`, killed by SIGKILL (too much memory, or `docker stop` ran out of patience); `143`, stopped by SIGTERM. `docker inspect` gives `State`, `Config.Cmd`, `Mounts` and the effective `Env`.

**What is Docker doing?** `docker events` shows, live, each time a container is created, started, exits, is killed for using too much memory, or changes health status.

**A container that crashes on start** can't be `exec`ed. Start the same image with a shell instead of its command: `docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myimage`, then run the real command by hand and watch it fail.

**Images without a shell** (distroless, scratch): start a separate container full of tools that shares the target's network and list of processes (its Linux namespaces, explained in the Expert lessons). `docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api nicolaka/netshoot` shares its network and its list of processes, so `curl localhost:8000`, `ss -lntp` and `ps` work against the target. Recent Docker Desktop versions offer `docker debug api`, which does this with a toolbox shell.

**Files**: `docker cp api:/app/log.txt .` copies out; `docker diff api` lists what changed in the writable layer.

**Network checklist** for "can't connect": same user-defined network? Using the service name, not `localhost`? Listening on `0.0.0.0`? Port published if the caller is outside Docker? `docker network inspect` and `nslookup` from a netshoot container answer each one.

**Build failures**: rerun with `--progress=plain --no-cache`, or build up to the failing stage with `--target` and run it interactively.
concepts.code:
docker ps -a --filter name=api --format '{{.Status}}'   # Exited (127) 3s ago
docker logs --tail 50 api
docker inspect api --format '{{json .Config.Cmd}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}'
docker events --filter container=api --since 10m

# Crash on start: get a shell in the same image instead
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh acme/api:1.4.2

# No shell in the image: borrow its network + PID namespaces
docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api \
  nicolaka/netshoot
#   ss -lntp ; curl -v localhost:8000/healthz ; ps aux

docker diff api            # A /tmp/x  C /etc  D /app/old.conf
docker cp api:/app/logs/error.log ./error.log
takeaways: Exit codes: 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM
--entrypoint sh opens a shell in an image whose container crashes
--network/--pid container:<name> attaches a tools container to a shell-less one
`docker events`, `inspect`, `diff` and `cp` round out the toolkit
pitfalls: Trying to docker exec into a container that has already exited — start a fresh one with --entrypoint sh instead.

quiz.q: A container exits immediately with code 127. What is the most likely cause?
options: The command in CMD/ENTRYPOINT wasn't found in the image
The port is already in use
quiz.explain: 127 is the shell's 'command not found' code.

quiz.q: How can you run curl against a distroless container's localhost without changing its image?
options: Run a tools container with --network container:api
quiz.explain: Sharing the network namespace makes the target's localhost the tools container's localhost.

concepts.name: Compose for real projects
concepts.summary: Layer extra Compose files, and use profiles, health-gated start order, placeholders and compose watch, to run development and CI from one setup.
concepts.why: Many teams run their local setup, and tests of several services working together, on Compose; these features keep it manageable.
concepts.body:
Once a project grows, a single flat `compose.yaml` starts to strain. Compose has tools for that.

**Extra files.** `docker compose up` automatically combines `compose.override.yaml` with `compose.yaml`, the override winning. Put production-like settings in the base file and development conveniences (bind mounts of your code, extra ports for inspecting the app) in `compose.override.yaml`. For other setups, pass files explicitly: `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml up`. Later files replace or add to settings from earlier ones.

**Profiles.** Mark optional services with `profiles: [tools]`; they start only with `--profile tools`. Good for admin web pages, scripts that fill the database with sample data, and load testers.

**Startup ordering.** `depends_on` conditions: `service_started`, `service_healthy` (requires a healthcheck) and `service_completed_successfully`, which is ideal for one-off jobs, such as updating the database's structure, that must finish before the app starts.

**Placeholders.** `${VAR}`, `${VAR:-default}` and `${VAR:?error message}` (stop with that message if unset) are filled in from your terminal session or the project's `.env`. Check the final, merged result with `docker compose config`; it's the best debugging tool for Compose files.

**Watch mode.** A `develop.watch` section plus `docker compose watch` copies changed code files into running containers (`action: sync`), restarts after settings changes (`sync+restart`) or rebuilds when dependencies change (`rebuild`). It replaces slow, fragile bind mounts on Docker Desktop.

**Reuse.** `include:` pulls in other Compose files, such as a shared infrastructure stack, and YAML anchors (a YAML way to reuse a section) or `extends` remove repetition.

**CI.** `docker compose up -d --wait` waits until services are healthy, and `docker compose run --rm tests` runs one-off containers on the project network.
concepts.code:
services:
  migrate:
    build: .
    command: ["alembic", "upgrade", "head"]
    depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["127.0.0.1:${API_PORT:-8000}:8000"]
    environment:
      SECRET_KEY: ${SECRET_KEY:?set SECRET_KEY in .env}
    depends_on:
      migrate: { condition: service_completed_successfully }
    develop:
      watch:
        - { action: sync, path: ./src, target: /app/src }
        - { action: rebuild, path: requirements.txt }
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"], interval: 5s }
  adminer:
    image: adminer
    profiles: [tools]
# docker compose config ; docker compose watch ; docker compose --profile tools up -d
takeaways: compose.override.yaml is merged automatically; -f stacks files explicitly
profiles make services optional; service_completed_successfully gates on jobs
docker compose config shows the fully merged, interpolated file
compose watch syncs or rebuilds on file changes
pitfalls: Debugging a confusing setup without running docker compose config to see what Compose actually resolved.

quiz.q: Which depends_on condition fits a database migration job that must finish before the API starts?
quiz.explain: It waits for the dependency to run to completion with exit code 0.

quiz.q: You run docker compose up in a folder with compose.yaml and compose.override.yaml. What is used?
options: Both, with the override merged on top
quiz.explain: Compose loads the override file automatically when no -f is given.

concepts.name: Namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Containers are built from Linux namespaces (what a process can see) and cgroups (what it can use).
concepts.why: Knowing the kernel features underneath explains a container's walls, its limits and many container bugs.
concepts.body:
There is no "container" thing in the Linux kernel. A container is an ordinary process set up with two families of kernel features.

**Linux namespaces** control what a process can **see**. Each kind gives the process its own private version of one thing the whole system shares:

- `pid`: its own list of processes; the app is PID 1 and can't see the host's processes.
- `net`: its own network: connections, IP addresses, ports and rules for where to send traffic (a pair of virtual cables, a veth pair, links it to the bridge network).
- `mnt`: its own list of attached storage, with the image's files as `/`.
- `uts`: its own computer name. `ipc`: its own shared memory that processes use to talk to each other.
- `user`: maps user IDs inside to different ones outside; this **user namespace** lets the container's root be a powerless user on the host (used by rootless mode and userns-remap, in the last lesson).
- `cgroup` and `time`: private versions of the cgroup tree and of some clocks.

Docker's flags map straight onto these: `--network host` and `--pid host` mean *don't* create that namespace, and `--network container:x` *joins* another container's namespace.

**Control groups (cgroups)** control what a process can **use**: memory, CPU time, how fast it reads and writes the disk, and number of processes, and they measure each. Modern hosts use **cgroup v2**, one tree of folders under `/sys/fs/cgroup`. When systemd (the program that starts and supervises services on most Linux systems) manages cgroups, a container lives in a folder like `system.slice/docker-<id>.scope`, where files such as `memory.max`, `cpu.max` and `pids.max` hold the limits you set with `--memory`, `--cpus` and `--pids-limit`.

Since a container is just a process, the host sees it: `ps` on the host lists it with a host PID, and `nsenter` can enter its namespaces. Together with Linux capabilities, seccomp and security add-ons such as AppArmor and SELinux (all in the last lesson), these features make up a container's walls, all on one shared kernel.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name web --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 nginx:1.27
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web)
ps -o pid,user,cmd -p "$PID"            # visible from the host
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns                # net -> net:[4026532301] ...
sudo lsns -p "$PID"

# Enter just its network namespace with host tools
sudo nsenter -t "$PID" -n ip addr

# Its cgroup v2 limits (systemd driver)
CG=$(awk -F: '{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)
cat /sys/fs/cgroup$CG/memory.max        # 268435456
cat /sys/fs/cgroup$CG/cpu.max           # 50000 100000
takeaways: Namespaces limit what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup, time
cgroups limit and account what it uses: memory, CPU, I/O, PIDs
--network host / container:x skip or share a namespace
A container is a host process; `nsenter` and `/proc` reveal it
pitfalls: Treating namespace isolation as a security boundary equal to a VM — all containers share one kernel.

quiz.q: Which mechanism enforces --memory 256m?
quiz.explain: cgroups limit resource usage; namespaces only change visibility.

quiz.q: What does docker run --pid host do?
options: Gives the container its own PID 1
Hides the host's processes more strongly
Skips creating a PID namespace, so the container sees all host processes
quiz.explain: Host mode means the container shares the host's namespace instead of getting a new one.

concepts.name: Union filesystems and overlayfs
concepts.summary: How overlayfs stacks read-only image layers under a writable container layer, with copy-up and whiteouts.
concepts.why: It explains layer sharing, slow first writes to big files and why data belongs in volumes.
concepts.body:
A container's files come from several folders stacked so they appear as one (a "union" of them). On Linux, Docker does this with the kernel's **overlayfs** feature, either through its classic `overlay2` storage engine or, with the containerd image store, containerd's equivalent. `docker info` shows which.

An overlay mount has:

- `lowerdir`: one or more read-only directories, the image layers, stacked top to bottom.
- `upperdir`: the container's writable layer.
- `workdir`: scratch space the kernel needs so that each change happens completely or not at all.
- `merged`: the combined result, which becomes the container's `/`.

Reads fall through the pile: the topmost layer that has a file wins. Because lower layers are read-only and identified by their contents, a hundred containers from the same image share one copy on disk and in memory.

Writes follow **copy-on-write** (copy something only at the moment it's changed):

- Modifying a file from a lower layer first causes a **copy-up**: the *whole* file is copied into upperdir, then modified. The first write to a 2 GB file copies 2 GB. That's one reason databases and other write-heavy data belong on volumes, which bypass the overlay entirely.
- Deleting a lower file creates a **whiteout** in upperdir, a special marker file that hides it; the data still exists below.
- Replacing a directory uses an **opaque** marker so lower contents are hidden.

Image layers work the same way at build time: each layer is stored as a tar archive (one file bundling many) of additions plus whiteout entries (`.wh.<name>`). That's why deleting files in a later Dockerfile step never shrinks an image.

Inspect a container's overlay with `docker inspect -f '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}'` (overlay2 driver) or `mount | grep overlay`.
concepts.code:
docker info --format '{{.Driver}}'          # overlay2 (or overlayfs via containerd)
docker run -d --name t alpine sleep 1d
docker inspect t --format '{{json .GraphDriver.Data}}' | tr ',' '\n'
# "LowerDir":"/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>-init/diff:/var/lib/docker/overlay2/<layer>/diff"
# "MergedDir":".../merged"  "UpperDir":".../diff"  "WorkDir":".../work"

docker exec t sh -c 'echo x >> /etc/hosts.allow; rm /etc/motd'
UPPER=$(docker inspect t --format '{{.GraphDriver.Data.UpperDir}}')
sudo ls -l "$UPPER/etc"
# -rw-r--r-- ... hosts.allow    <- copied up, then modified
# c--------- 0, 0 ... motd       <- whiteout hiding the lower file
docker diff t                    # C /etc  A /etc/hosts.allow  D /etc/motd
takeaways: `lowerdir` = read-only image layers, `upperdir` = container layer, `merged` = /
First write to a lower file copies the whole file up
Deletes are whiteouts; the data stays in the lower layer
Write-heavy data belongs on volumes, outside the overlay
pitfalls: Storing a large, frequently written file (like a small database file) in the image and paying for copy-up plus the slower overlay in every container.

quiz.q: A container appends one line to a 1 GB log file that came from the image. What does overlayfs do?
options: Writes only the new line to the upper layer
Copies the entire 1 GB file to the upper layer, then appends
Modifies the image layer in place
Fails because image layers are read-only
quiz.explain: Copy-up operates on whole files on first write.

quiz.q: How does overlayfs represent a file deleted in the container but present in the image?
options: A whiteout entry in the upper layer hides it
The file is removed from the lower layer
It isn't possible to delete it
quiz.explain: Lower layers are never modified; a whiteout masks the file in the merged view.

concepts.name: OCI image and runtime specs
concepts.summary: Under the OCI standards, an image is a set of files named by their fingerprints (index, manifest, config, layers), and runc starts containers from a bundle.
concepts.why: The open specs are why images built by Docker run on Kubernetes, Podman and any registry.
concepts.body:
The **Open Container Initiative** (OCI) defines three specifications that make containers portable between tools.

The **image spec** describes an image as a set of stored files, each named by its `sha256` digest, so changing one byte changes the name. Every pointer to one of them gives its type, digest and size:

- An **image index** lists manifests per platform (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`), plus, in images built by buildx, extra entries describing the image, such as its SBOM and a signed note of how it was built.
- An **image manifest** describes one image: it points to one **config** file and an ordered list of **layer** files.
- The **config** JSON holds the starting settings (`Entrypoint`, `Cmd`, `Env`, `User`, `WorkingDir`), the history, and the `rootfs.diff_ids`: digests of the *uncompressed* layers.
- **Layers** are tar archives of file changes (with whiteouts), usually compressed with gzip or zstd; the manifest's digest for each is calculated on the compressed version.

The image's digest is the fingerprint of its manifest (or image index). Since the manifest names every file by fingerprint, one digest fixes every byte. Docker's own v2 manifest format is a near twin and both are accepted everywhere.

The **distribution spec** defines how programs talk to a registry over the web, with requests such as `GET /v2/<name>/manifests/<reference>` and `GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>`, and uploads in pieces. Registries now also store things other than images, such as Helm charts (app packages for Kubernetes), SBOMs and digital seals proving who built an image, attached to an image through a `subject` entry.

The **runtime spec** defines a **bundle**: a folder holding the container's files plus a `config.json` describing the process to start, its mounts, Linux namespaces, cgroups, Linux capabilities and seccomp rules, and the steps of its life (create, start, kill, delete). **runc** is the standard program that carries it out; Docker turns the image's config plus your `docker run` options into that `config.json`.
concepts.code:
# Index -> per-platform manifests
docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw nginx:1.27 | head -20
# {"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
#  "manifests":[{"digest":"sha256:...","platform":{"architecture":"amd64","os":"linux"}}, ...]}

# One manifest: config + layers (crane is a small registry CLI)
crane manifest --platform linux/arm64 nginx:1.27
# {"config":{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json","digest":"sha256:..."},
#  "layers":[{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip","digest":"sha256:...","size":29136913}, ...]}

crane config nginx:1.27 | jq '.config.Cmd, .rootfs.diff_ids[0]'

# Generate a runtime-spec config.json
mkdir bundle && cd bundle && runc spec && jq '.process.args, .linux.namespaces' config.json
takeaways: Index -> manifest -> config + layers, all addressed by sha256 digest
The image digest is the manifest's fingerprint, fixing every byte
Distribution spec = registry HTTP API; registries also store artifacts
Runtime spec = rootfs + config.json, executed by runc
pitfalls: Comparing layer digests from the manifest with config diff_ids — one is of compressed bytes, the other uncompressed, so they differ.

quiz.q: What is a multi-platform image tag at the registry level?
options: One manifest containing every architecture's layers
An image index pointing to one manifest per platform
A compressed tar of all images
quiz.explain: The index lists per-platform manifests; clients pick the matching one.

quiz.q: Why does pinning an image by digest guarantee identical contents?
options: The digest is a hash of the manifest, which names every blob by hash
quiz.explain: Content addressing chains hashes from manifest to config and layers.

concepts.name: Engine architecture: dockerd, containerd, runc
concepts.summary: Follow docker run through the CLI, dockerd, containerd, the shim and runc, and see why each layer exists.
concepts.why: Knowing the pieces explains what survives a daemon restart, how other container engines plug in, and how Kubernetes relates to Docker.
concepts.body:
`docker run` passes through several components, each with a narrow job.

- **docker CLI**: a client that sends requests to the daemon through the **Docker socket**, `/var/run/docker.sock` (or to another computer's daemon, chosen with `DOCKER_HOST` or contexts).
- **dockerd**: the Docker Engine. It owns the features you use: answering the CLI, image builds (through BuildKit), networks, volumes, Compose support and storing container output.
- **containerd**: a separate background program that manages images, layer storage and each container's life from start to finish. Kubernetes talks to containerd directly through its own plug-in standard (CRI), which is why Kubernetes could remove its Docker-specific connector ("dockershim"), and why the headlines about Kubernetes leaving Docker behind changed little for images.
- **containerd-shim-runc-v2**, the **containerd shim**: one small helper per container. It becomes the container's parent process, holds its input, output and exit code, and lets dockerd and containerd restart without killing containers (turn on `live-restore` in `daemon.json` for the full effect).
- **runc**: the OCI runtime. It reads the bundle's `config.json`, creates the Linux namespaces and cgroups, applies Linux capabilities, seccomp and mounts, starts the container's main process, then **exits**. It is not a long-running daemon.

Because runc is one replaceable piece, you can swap it per container: `--runtime runsc` (gVisor, which puts an imitation kernel in between for stronger walls), Kata Containers (each container in a lightweight VM) or other runc-compatible programs such as crun or youki. `docker info` shows the available ones and the default.

Tools exist at each level: `ctr` and `nerdctl` talk to containerd directly, and `runc list` shows what runc knows about. Docker namespaces its containers in containerd as `moby`, so `sudo ctr -n moby containers ls` lists them.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name demo nginx:1.27
ps -o pid,ppid,cmd -C containerd-shim-runc-v2,nginx
#   PID  PPID CMD
#  4120     1 /usr/bin/containerd-shim-runc-v2 -namespace moby -id 5c1e...
#  4141  4120 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;

sudo ctr -n moby containers ls          # same container, seen by containerd
docker info --format '{{.DefaultRuntime}} {{json .Runtimes}}'

# /etc/docker/daemon.json: keep containers running across daemon restarts
#   { "live-restore": true }
sudo systemctl restart docker && docker ps   # demo is still up

docker run --rm --runtime runsc alpine uname -a   # if gVisor is installed
takeaways: CLI -> dockerd (API, builds, networks) -> containerd -> shim -> runc
runc sets up the container and exits; the shim stays as its parent
Shims plus live-restore keep containers alive across daemon restarts
Runtimes are pluggable: gVisor, Kata, crun via --runtime
pitfalls: Opening the Docker socket to the network without encryption and client certificates: anyone who connects gets administrator control of the host.

quiz.q: Which component remains the parent process of a running container after it starts?
quiz.explain: runc exits after creating the container; the shim supervises it.

quiz.q: Kubernetes removed dockershim. Why do images built with Docker still run on it?
options: They are OCI images, and containerd/CRI-O run OCI images
Docker is still embedded in kubelet
They don't; images must be rebuilt
quiz.explain: Images follow the OCI spec, so any compliant runtime can run them.

concepts.name: Rootless mode, capabilities and seccomp
concepts.summary: Reduce container privileges with removed capabilities, seccomp, no-new-privileges, user namespaces and rootless Docker.
concepts.why: Defence in depth turns a container compromise into a contained incident instead of a host takeover.
concepts.body:
Root, the administrator, in a container is the host's own user ID 0 (unless user namespaces are used), held back by several separate protections. Knowing them lets you tighten each.

**Linux capabilities** split the administrator's power into separate permissions. Docker grants a reduced default set (including `CHOWN`, `DAC_OVERRIDE`, `SETUID`, `SETGID`, `NET_BIND_SERVICE`, `NET_RAW`, `KILL`) and withholds dangerous ones like `SYS_ADMIN`, `SYS_MODULE` and `NET_ADMIN`. Best practice: `--cap-drop ALL`, then `--cap-add` only what's needed.

**seccomp** filters **system calls**, the requests a program makes to the kernel (such as "open this file"). Docker's default profile forbids dozens of risky ones (loading add-ons into the kernel, `reboot`, `kexec_load`, `mount` without the right capability...) while allowing what normal apps use. Custom profiles go in with `--security-opt seccomp=profile.json`. Never use `seccomp=unconfined` casually.

**`--security-opt no-new-privileges`** stops programs marked to run with extra rights (setuid programs and file capabilities) from giving a process more power than it started with.

**Security add-ons**: AppArmor (its `docker-default` profile) or SELinux labels add extra kernel-enforced rules about which files and mounts a process may touch.

**`--privileged`** turns nearly all of this off: all capabilities, all devices, no seccomp. It is effectively host root, so avoid it outside special situations such as running Docker inside Docker or direct hardware access.

**User namespaces** remap container root to an unprivileged host UID. `userns-remap` in `daemon.json` does this for all containers. **Rootless mode** goes further: the daemon itself runs as a normal user (`dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install`), using a range of spare user IDs set aside in `/etc/subuid`, and a helper called RootlessKit for networking. A full escape then yields only that user's rights. Trade-offs: using ports below 1024 needs a kernel setting changed (with sysctl), and some networking and storage features are limited.

Combine these with a non-root `USER` and `--read-only` for strong defaults.
concepts.code:
docker run -d --name api \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -p 80:80 acme/api:1.4.2

docker inspect api --format '{{.HostConfig.CapDrop}} {{.HostConfig.SecurityOpt}}'
docker run --rm alpine grep Cap /proc/self/status     # default capability bitmasks

# Rootless Docker for the current user
dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
export DOCKER_HOST=unix://$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/docker.sock
docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'   # [name=seccomp,... name=rootless ...]
takeaways: Remove all capabilities and add back only what's needed
The default seccomp profile forbids risky system calls; don't run unconfined
--privileged disables almost all isolation
userns-remap or rootless mode map container root to an unprivileged host user
pitfalls: Reaching for --privileged to fix a permission error instead of adding the single capability or device actually required.

quiz.q: Which flag most effectively removes root powers a web app doesn't need?
quiz.explain: Dropping every capability then adding back only what's needed minimises privilege.

quiz.q: In rootless mode, what does root inside a container correspond to on the host?
options: The unprivileged user running the rootless daemon (via user namespaces)
quiz.explain: Rootless Docker maps container UIDs into that user's subordinate UID range.
